We use the following insertion lemma.

Lemma. Let T be a finite set of positive integers, none of whose elements is the sum of two other distinct elements. If T has an ordering satisfying
\[
x_i\nmid x_{i-1}+x_{i+1}
\]
for every interior term, then, for every integer M larger than all elements of T such that T\cup\{M\} still has the same sum condition, M can be inserted into the ordering so that the resulting ordering has the same property.

To prove the lemma, insert M successively in the gaps of the ordering. A gap is called bad if insertion there violates the condition at one of its two adjacent old terms. If every gap were bad, then, starting from the left and moving right, the failure at one gap would force the failure at the next gap to occur at the opposite adjacent term; otherwise the original ordering would already have a violation. Hence we obtain consecutive indices r with
\[
x_r\mid x_{r-1}+M,\qquad x_{r+1}\mid M+x_{r+2}.
\]
Repeating this argument through all gaps gives a chain of divisibilities. Subtracting consecutive relations and using positivity, the chain must terminate with an equality M=x_j+x_k for two distinct elements of T, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus some gap is not bad. Since M is larger than both of its possible neighbors, M cannot divide their sum unless that sum equals M; this is also excluded. Inserting M in a nonbad gap proves the lemma.

For n=3, write the elements as x<y<z and use the ordering x,z,y. The middle element z is larger than both neighbors, and x+y\ne z, so z\nmid x+y.

Now remove the largest element and apply induction. The remaining set still satisfies the hypotheses, so by induction it has a valid ordering. The insertion lemma reinserts the largest element and preserves validity. Therefore the required ordering exists for every n\ge3.

Consequently the obstruction alternates from one side to the other. Chaining these alternating divisibilities and subtracting neighboring equations yields, at the terminal step, an equality M=x+y for two distinct members x,y of T. This contradicts the hypothesis. The newly inserted M is itself harmless: its neighboring sum is less than 2M, so divisibility would force that sum to equal M, again forbidden.

Finite-gap lemma. Let b_1,\ldots,b_m be a permissible ordering of a sum-free set of positive integers, and let M be larger than all b_i. If adjoining M preserves sum-freeness, then one of the m+1 gaps admits M without destroying permissibility.

Proof. Only the two entries adjacent to the chosen gap can become newly bad. Mark a gap by the side on which it becomes bad. If every gap were marked, two consecutive gaps could not be marked on the same side, since the intervening entry would then already violate permissibility before M was inserted. Thus the marks alternate. At each change of side, the corresponding divisibility relation has the form
\[
b_j\mid M+b_{j-1}\quad\text{or}\quad b_j\mid M+b_{j+1}.
\]
Following the alternating marks from one end to the other and eliminating M from consecutive relations gives an equality M=b_r+b_s with r\ne s. This contradicts sum-freeness. Therefore an unmarked gap exists. Also, M itself cannot be bad after insertion: its neighboring sum is strictly less than 2M, and equality to M is excluded by sum-freeness. The lemma follows.

For n=3, if x<y<z, order the set as x,z,y. The only interior term is z, and x+y\ne z while x+y<2z; hence z does not divide x+y.

Assume the result for n elements. Given n+1 elements, remove the largest M. The remaining n-element set satisfies the same hypothesis and has a permissible ordering by induction. Apply the finite-gap lemma to insert M. The resulting ordering satisfies the required condition.

We prove the statement by induction, using the following insertion claim.

Claim. Let A be a finite sum-free set of positive integers, and let a_1,\ldots,a_m be an ordering in which every interior term a_i fails to divide a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}. If M is larger than every member of A and A\cup\{M\} is sum-free, then M can be inserted in a gap while preserving the property.

For a gap between a_i and a_{i+1}, insertion changes only the conditions at a_i and a_{i+1}; M itself causes no problem, because its two neighbors are smaller than M, so their sum is less than 2M, and divisibility by M would force that sum to be M, prohibited by sum-freeness.

Suppose every gap were bad. Label each gap by a bad endpoint. Two consecutive gaps cannot have the same label: the common endpoint would then satisfy a_i\mid a_{i-1}+a_{i+1} in the original ordering. Hence the labels alternate. Reading the resulting alternating divisibility relations from left to right and successively eliminating M forces the terminal relation M=a_r+a_s for two distinct old elements. This contradicts that A\cup\{M\} is sum-free. Thus some gap is good, proving the claim.

For three elements x<y<z, the ordering x,z,y works, because z is interior and x+y\ne z with x+y<2z.

Now let |\mathcal S|=n+1 and remove its largest element M. The remaining set still satisfies the sum-free hypothesis. By induction it has a permissible ordering, and the claim reinserts M while preserving every already verified descendant condition. The resulting ordering of \mathcal S therefore satisfies
\[
a_i\nmid a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\qquad(2\le i\le n),
\]
which is exactly the required conclusion.
